The nagada is a drum used in India, classified as a membranophone. The common form is a pair of drums, one higher and one lower, struck with sticks; in South Indian temple ritual and at weddings it is treated as the leading instrument. The lower half of the body is a hemispherical metal vessel, the head is covered with hide and fixed with rope or metal strips, and it is struck with a special stick or a bent rod. There is also a single-headed large ritual drum, seen in gatka performances in the Sikh tradition and once used on the battlefield. In Central Asia and the Middle East it is usually treated as a single drum, with different names by size. In temples in Tamil Nadu the drum is handled by temple staff and used for daily worship, consecrations, temple fairs, festivals and processions, announcing the progress of the ritual to the public by its rhythm.
納加達鼓為膜鳴樂器，發聲體為蒙皮膜。來源記載其底部為半球形金屬容器，金屬部分可能: The nagada is a membranophone whose sounding body is a skin membrane. The source records that the base is a hemispherical metal vessel, the metal possibly brass or copper; the head is usually goatskin or similar leather, fixed to the vessel with rope or metal strips. It is played with a special beater or a bent wooden rod, whose material is not stated. The source does not describe the materials of the rest of the body, the fittings or the fixings either.
納加達鼓起源於埃及納加達古城，該城位於尼羅河西岸，距盧克索北部約二十公里，是古埃: The nagada takes its name from the ancient city of Nagada in Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile about twenty kilometres north of Luxor, an important cultural centre of ancient Egyptian civilisation. The Nagada area holds some two thousand ancient tombs, evidence of a long musical tradition in ancient Egypt. The drum developed and was refined through the ancient Egyptian period and became an important instrument of religious ritual and popular celebration.

隨著時間推移，納加達鼓的製作技藝得以保留並傳承。該地區的科普特基督教社群長期居住: Over time the craft of making the nagada has been kept and passed on. The Coptic Christian community lived in the area until the 1930s, and it preserved the traditional craft and the music-making of the nagada. By modern times the drum has gone beyond its own region and become a percussion instrument widely used across the Middle East and North Africa. Its distinctive timbre and playing technique have gradually become known to enthusiasts of world music, and it holds an important place in the folk-music revival, standing for the link between ancient Egyptian civilisation and modern culture.
